name: Killer Sudoku Puzzles Are Sound (cages, sums, one solution, levels)
note: Written with the gate on 2026-10-01, with the killer engine itself. Each mutation breaks one promise a killer puzzle makes to the player.

mutations.name: the generator ships the first cut without asking if it has one answer
mutations.why: The promise itself. A cut with two answers is accepted, and a player who fills in the other answer is told they are wrong. The gate counts answers with its own brute force, so the generator cannot mark its own work.
mutations.find: if (result.count === 1 && !result.aborted && guesses <= config.guesses) return { cages, givens, guesses };
mutations.expectFailure: a killer must have exactly one solution

mutations.name: the level's limit on wrong turns is dropped
mutations.why: Puzzles stay unique but any of them may need a long chain of guesses; a Lv.4 measured at 1,902 wrong turns before the cap, and on today's ladder a Lv.5 seed takes 461 without it (the ladder's Expert peaks near 155). The level stops meaning anything.
mutations.find: if (result.count === 1 && !result.aborted && guesses <= config.guesses) return { cages, givens, guesses };

mutations.name: a cage may take a cell whose digit it already holds
mutations.why: The rule of a cage: no digit twice. Such a cage contradicts the grid it was cut from, so the solver finds no answer and the generator refuses to ship it — that refusal is what this proves. The gate's own digit check is proven by faking the shipped solution, below.
mutations.expectFailure: lost the solution it was cut from

mutations.name: a cage's sum is one more than its digits
mutations.why: The number in the corner is the whole puzzle. Off by one, the grid it was cut from no longer solves it, and the generator refuses to ship it. The gate's own sum check is proven by faking the shipped sums, below.
mutations.find: return { cells: sorted, sum: sorted.reduce((sum, c) => sum + digit[c], 0) };
mutations.replace: return { cells: sorted, sum: sorted.reduce((sum, c) => sum + digit[c], 1) };
mutations.expectFailure: lost the solution it was cut from

mutations.name: a split cage keeps its far-apart leftovers as one cage
mutations.why: Splitting can leave cells of a cage that no longer touch. Kept together, one dashed outline is drawn around two islands and the player cannot tell which cells it means.
mutations.find: for (const n of neighbours(piece[i])) if (left.delete(n)) piece.push(n);

mutations.name: the seed is ignored
mutations.why: Two players given the same seed get different puzzles; a daily killer would differ from phone to phone.
mutations.expectFailure: the same seed gave two different puzzles

mutations.name: Lv.3 goes back to four digits
mutations.why: Before 2026-10-07 the killer "Medium" gave 4-7 digits and played between Easybrain's Hard and Expert; a player who picked Medium got something much harder. The gate pins the ladder measured on that app, so the numbers cannot drift back.

mutations.name: Lv.3 goes back to its big cages
mutations.why: The old Lv.3 aimed for three- to five-cell cages and averaged 2.97 cells; bigger cages hold more possible sets of digits and are harder. Easybrain cuts every level the same, about 2.45 cells.

mutations.name: Lv.4 repairs by revealing digits
mutations.why: Lv.4 is the ladder's Hard: ten digits, no more. Revealing digits to make the answer unique would hand the player extra ones, a Hard drifting toward Medium.

mutations.name: a given may land on a one-cell cage
mutations.why: A one-cell cage already shows its digit; a given on it is one of the level's digits wasted, so the puzzle plays harder than its count says. Easybrain never does it.
mutations.find: for (const cell of shuffle([...Array(81).keys()].filter((c) => !single.has(c)), rng).slice(0, config.givens)) reveal(cell);
mutations.replace: for (const cell of shuffle([...Array(81).keys()], rng).slice(0, config.givens)) reveal(cell);
mutations.expectFailure: a given on a one-cell cage

mutations.name: a given a split leaves alone stays where it is
mutations.why: Lv.4 repairs by splitting cages around its ten givens; a split can leave a given alone in a one-cell cage, which already shows the digit. Kept there, 6% of Lv.4 puzzles play with nine givens. Found 2026-10-07 only because the seed mutation made the puzzles random.
mutations.expectFailure: a split left it alone and it was not moved

mutations.name: the 45 rule adds up to 44
mutations.why: The solver's 45 rule is how it narrows a killer with no digits given; adding wrongly, it throws out the real answer and proves the wrong things.
mutations.find: if (rest.size > 0 && rest.size < 9) out.push({ cells: [...rest], sum: 45 - covered });
mutations.replace: if (rest.size > 0 && rest.size < 9) out.push({ cells: [...rest], sum: 44 - covered });

mutations.name: the solver takes a digit seen twice in a row for one with a single place
mutations.why: An unsound narrowing step: the solver throws out digits that belong. The gate's open puzzle — a whole row in each cage, which every sudoku fits — comes back with no solution at all. (The first version of this mutation set lone = once, which changes nothing — every candidate of a cell is in `once` — and survived for that reason.)

mutations.name: the solver never reports more than one solution
mutations.why: A solver that stops at the first answer calls every puzzle unique. The gate gives it a puzzle with a whole row in each cage, which fits every sudoku there is.
mutations.replace: return { count: Math.min(count, 1), solutions, aborted, nodes };
mutations.expectFailure: would call an open puzzle unique

mutations.name: the shipped puzzle says one more on its first cage
mutations.why: A wrong number in a corner that the generator never checked — written after the work was done. The gate reads every sum against the solution itself.
mutations.replace: cages: cages.map((cage, i) => (i ? cage : { ...cage, sum: cage.sum + 1 })),

mutations.name: the shipped solution repeats a digit in the first cage
mutations.why: The solution the hint button and the mistake check read from has the same digit twice in one cage; the player is told a correct cage is wrong. The gate reads every cage against the solution itself.
mutations.replace: solution: solution.map((row, r) => row.map((d, c) => (r * 9 + c === cages[0].cells[1] ? solution[0][0] : d))),

mutations.name: a cut that decayed into one-cell cages is shipped
mutations.why: Added 2026-10-06. Lv.4-5 are cages only, but splitting pairs can leave a dozen or more one-cell cages, each a given drawn as a cage: 13 in 300 Lv.5 puzzles went past 12, up to 18. The generator cuts again; without that the gate's fixed decayed seed fails.
mutations.expectFailure: a decayed cut was shipped instead of cut again

mutations.name: a cut that needed too many extra digits is shipped
mutations.why: One Lv.3 in 1000 took thirteen extra digits to become unique — a Medium holding more digits than Lv.1. Such a cut must be cut again.
mutations.expectFailure: too many extra digits was shipped instead of cut again
